But it must be realized that they work not over thirty-four hours a week and less than twenty-nine hours in the summer months. Yet we have a group of civil servants in the penitentiaries who at times take their lives in their hands, working forty-eight hours a week. It is little wonder that they complain and say,
' Why should we be treated in this way while others employed by the same government are working the short hours they are". I am not complaining about the civil service because the tendency today is toward fewer hours of work.
I now wish to put on the record the salaries that engineers in both of these establishments receive. In the provincial institutions engineers receive S260 to S296 a month, whereas we are paying the same class of engineers $210. These men are also training convicts. I had it drawn to my attention that last year nine convicts received fourth-class certificates from the tuition received at the hands of the teachers or instructors in the penitentiaries, and at least two of them went out and procured positions at a higher salary than that received by their instructors. That may be an isolated case, but bear in mind that industrial plants and provincial governments themselves pay higher wages and offer greater inducements to employees than does the dominion government. It is little wonder that many of our people are attracted or lured away across the line where more is offered for the services which they can give. At a later date when the civil service estimates are before the house I want to go into this more fully than I have done tonight, because I realize I have touched only but one branch of the service, namely, those employed in the penitentiaries.
I should now like to refer for a moment to postal matters. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) raised the point the other day and asked whether a committee was to be
set up to investigate rural mail routes. I am bringing this matter up not for the purpose of creating jealousy or to suggest that we do things in a bigger and better way in British Columbia, but I can tell hon. members from the other provinces that the rural routes in British Columbia are larger than those of the other provinces. The number of boxes on rural routes out there are astounding, when compared with those in the other provinces.
I have before me some of the rural routes in my own district. On one route a man handles each day 687 individual letter boxes. There are seven routes, and on the seven routes there are a total of 3.923 mail boxes. That is the last count I have. I am told that in Ontario and Quebec a route which has sixty or sixty-five boxes is considered to be a good one; yet we have in British Columbia the fastest-growing province in the dominion. I say this particularly to my hon. friends from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We have been few in number for a long time; but British Columbia is growing at such a rate that it will not be long before we shall be sending down as many members as either of the two older provinces. I am not going to say why the people are leaving the other provinces to come to our province, but we have increased so rapidly that since the last census our population has increased from
817,000	to nearly 1,500,000, and in another fifteen years or so we may have three million people out there. When we have the number of members coming to this house to represent that population you will then hear more about British Columbia. That. is not a threat, Mr. Speaker; it is just a plain statement of fact.
I have just one more suggestion to offer before I resume my seat. I am asking the government to give some consideration to amending the Farm Loan Act which was put into force many years ago. But conditions have changed since that time, and it should be amended. Under the Farm Loan Act today a first mortgage loan is restricted to $5,000 plus another $1,000, making a total of $6,000. In the light of building costs and the like today, I believe these loans should be increased to $10,000. The value of barns and farm buildings in general has increased. Nothing was done during the war years to take care of barns or to keep them in repair. Under provincial regulations the provincial authorities are tightening up. They are going around the province condemning many of these buildings. A man on. a modern stock farm today requires a lot of money to put up a modern barn. Without a modern barn a
6S0
The Address-Mr. Miller

man cannot farm successfully. Therefore, I am asking that consideration be given to amendments to the Farm Loan Act.
Loans under the Farm Loan Act should also be for a longer time. Because of the shortage of help, our farms in British Columbia have become mechanized. The farmers are buying machinery. Conditions have compelled them to do that because labour has been reluctant to go on the farms, or it has been almost impossible to procure workers for the farms. Consequently the farmer has been purchasing machinery. Today you see one man or two men doing the farm work which was formerly done by eight, nine or ten men. Therefore I am asking that the loans under this act be provided for a longer period- than at present. Also the farm loan board, if they are in business at all, should go out after business andi advertise. If they do not do that, let us. consider winding up the Farm Loan Act and let the farmers get their loans elsewhere.
Perhaps I have spoken longer than I had intended, but I have just touched on a few of the local matters. At a later day I intend to deal with some other important matters.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. C. MILLER (Portage la Prairie):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite a while since the mover and the seconder moved the address in reply to the speech fro-m the throne, but not too long ago to enable me to recall the manner in which they performed their duties and to offer to them, as many other speakers have done and as it has become customary to do, my.sincere congratulations on their effort. Particularly I should like to congratulate the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) who, in his maiden speech, took part in this debate by seconding the motion for an address. None of us is too far removed from his maiden effort to forget the difficulties of t'he first speech; certainly not I, whose time in this house is still fairly close to that first dreadful day.
To the junior -member for Halifax I should like to say particularly that, as I sat here and listened to him, it was not difficult for me to offer my congratulations sincerely, and not simply as a matter of form.
Like many other speakers who have taken part in this and, may I say, other debates,
I should like to refer to the cost of living. The last speaker truly said that the cost of living is one of those issues which in recent months has, as we say in the west, like a prairie fire spread quickly across this nation and become more than a problem, almost an emergency.

I come from a locality in which there are not only a large number of farmers but also, scattered throughout that constituency, a large number of smaller towns and cities and villages. These towns are mostly rural towns; that is what we call them because, directly or indirectly, they are mainly dependent upon agriculture for their existence. In these towns scattered throughout my constituency there are many people who are in receipt of small incomes. In fact, I would say that over sixty per cent of the inhabitants of my native -city of Portage la Prairie are what might be termed small income or salary earners.
Under existing high cost of living conditions these people have no chance in the world of balancing the domestic or family budget. We see these men and women whom we have known all our lives going around and acquiring that worried look which we so well remember from the depression years of the thirties. That should not be; but whether it is the fault of this government that these conditions exist, or whether it is not, is beside the point. This fact must be self-evident, that the responsibility for curing that condition among the people is definitely the responsibility of those who are entrusted with power in this country.
The small income groups, the old age pensioners and those in receipt of veterans pensions and so on are all in the same position, if not worse. There is another group for whom I should like to say something tonight, and that is the civil servants. There are a large number of civil servants in the constituency I represent. Some of them are federal civil servants and some of them provincial, because we have several provincial institutions there.
There you see a group of people who have not been given an increase of any consequence since the war years. The high cost of living has sneaked up on them and, through no fault of their own, they have been practically bludgeoned into a position where they are unable to afford many things which they must have to keep body and soul together. It seems to me strange indeed that the employees of our government, above all people, should find themselves in this unsatisfactory position. It is a travesty. The increases announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the pre-Christmas sitting, were entirely inadequate, and on top of that there are countless hundreds to whom these increases do not apply.
What I object to and what I am trying to make clear is that every government, federal or provincial, knows full well that these men

The Address-Mr. Miller
are not getting enough to meet the cost of living, that they are not able to balance the family budget, that they are worried. In the name of all that is fair and just and right, I maintain that the government, whether federal or provincial, should immediately establish some sort of temporary bonus system to relieve the situation in which these people find themselves; and then, if it takes time to settle the procedure, if the government must dilly-dally in making the temporary arrangements permanent, it should be seen to that this delay will not be at the expense of these people, while governments are trying to establish a method of doing things, making up their mind what to do. While that is going on we should see to it that these people are relieved from worry and want.
We are told that relief both from indirect taxation and from income taxation would do more than put additional money in the hands of spenders and thus create more pressure on a rising market for scarce goods. I do not pretend to be a monetary expert or a specialist in economics, but I know that the people who require that assistance and who would benefit most from relief from indirect taxation and from a lifting of the income tax are those people who are in receipt of small incomes. They are not worrying about bringing pressure to bear on scarce goods; all they are worrying about is to get a little more money with which to buy food and clothing and pay rent. They will not put much pressure on scarce goods but they must be enabled to have a house to live in.
It does not take an economist to figure out that the course suggested by speakers in this party should be followed, namely, relief from indirect taxation and a reduction in income tax. It does not take an economist to realize that this course would not put pressure upon the purchasing of scarce articles, while it would make it easier for this class of small salaried people to have a little more money in order to balance the domestic budget.
Everybody on the government side of the house realizes that this is a bad situation throughout the country. As we go through these little towns and villages we find that business is becoming poor; that merchants are starting to complain of a falling off in trade; that unemployment is making its appearance once again, and that a demand is being made that local merchants give credit. That is only a small sign; but I maintain, economist or not, that it is the first sign, if not of depression, then of imminent recession. These are storm signals which the government must observe; for, if they do not observe them, we shall be
far into the cycle and we shall not be able to halt what may turn out to be a serious depression.
Unlike the last speaker, I cannot find it in my heart to praise the government for establishing or promising to establish or appoint a committee to investigate the cost of living. That, it seems to me, is only shifting the responsibility and is but a poor makeshift, a poor tool to use in coping with this great national emergency. It seems to me that the government have everything to guide them in deciding what they shall do or shall not do, or what they can do, because they have all the so-called experts at their beck and call. What more can they get from a committee? If there is a remedy the government should find it among their own employees, bring it in and tell us what will be done about the situation, or that situation will become not only a calamity but a national disgrace.
It would be difficult for me at this time to refrain from some reference to income tax. Again let me say that I do not for one minute profess to be a student of monetary affairs, but I have always been told and have understood that there is a danger point in taxation and, if that point is passed, immediately we start downhill. It is the first impetus to recession or depression, whatever you wish to call it. It is, I suggest, an axiom or a self-evident truth that we have long since, particularly in the matter of income tax, passed the danger point and it is time for a scaling down. This is particularly true at the moment of city and town people. The people in the cities and towns need what they pay in income tax to keep body and soul together. They have not enough money to balance their budgets and this would be a measure of relief to them. When they have not enough money to pay bills and doctors' bills they should not be subject to income tax.
It has been proven beyond question that we have reached the saturation point in taxation. But let us consider the farmers. As the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) said today, a new form is being spread among the farmers of western Canada. It is called the prairie fanners 1947 income tax return. Prairie farmers, Mr. Speaker! What does that mean? Does it mean that we are to perpetuate the difference which has long existed in taxation between the western farmer and the eastern farmer, or does it mean that the western farmer is of such and such a quality or breed that a special form must be used to track him and his resources down to the last tenth of a cent?
The form is all right. It is prepared unquestionably by able accountants. But I
The Address-Mr. Miller

ask you this question, Mr. Speaker: What form that a chartered accountant or trained accountant may prepare can a farmer fill out correctly? I often wonder if many of the men who serve under the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MeCan-n) ever saw a farm. They have a form here which would take the farmer all the Sundays in the year to fill out, and that is about the only time he has to spare.
In the practice of law in a rural western town I have had some experience with* returns for farmers. I know that you cannot make book-keepers out of them. I also know that the department, in their wisdom and in an endeavor to be helpful, sent out a book of instructions which nine out of ten farmers will lose during the first week they will have them. Nevertheless, that book is good; but I suggest that, in the distribution of these books throughout the length and breadth of the prairie provinces there should have been delivered with every one *of those books either a stenographer or a book-keeper. Perhaps the eastern farmers would like that too.
Now let me deal with this summary on the back page of this iniquitous form. May I say right now that I do not agree with the hon. member for Souris when he says that the department should hurry up the distribution of this form. I think they should recall every one of them, bring them in and burn them. There is not one of them worth anything to a farmer.
Here we have this summary. They are going to find out the net worth of the farmer, a man who proverbially is honest but is a poor book-keeper. Here are the first three questions on that statement:	The first is,
"Cash* on person or on farm". They even want to know what the farmer has in* his hip-pocket from day to day. The second question is, "Cash in bank". Well, there is nothing particularly wrong about that. I do not know whether or not any of them have cash in the bank now. I imagine some of them have. But here is the third question, and it is the pay-off question. They want to know, "Cash in safety deposit box at banks". Mr. Speaker, what sinister suggestion lies behind that question? Do they think the farmers of my native province are a bunch of crooks hiding their currency in safety deposit boxes in the banks to keep it from the income tax people? If not, why is that question in* there? Our farmers want to know why that question is there. Is it to be on the forms that are to be delivered to farmers in other parts of Canada, or is it the farmers of western Canada alone who must disclose if

they are stealing money and putting it in safety deposit boxes, and things like that? I do not think it is right.
From the experience I thought I had in making out these forms, I had occasion to write to the minister in protest, saying that if the department used these forms there would be considerable opposition among the farmers of the west with regard to making them out, not because the farmers particularly do not want to pay income tax, although none of us loves to pay it. Yet I think I am fair in saying that the western farmers hate making out these cursed forms more than they hate paying the income tax. They do not go in for bookkeeping. They do not know how to do it. These forms bother them to death. I suggested to the minister that they make these forms simpler and not try to go through with this, because they would get better cooperation from the farmers if they used a simpler form. However, the deputy minister wrote me back a nice letter in which he suggested that he thought perhaps I was one of those fellows who thought farmers should not pay income tax.
There is one thing being done in the farming communities in the west which is not bad; in fact, it is rather praise-worthy. Inspectors are being sent out, and they are holding meetings to explain this form. I do not think they can ever explain it to the satisfaction of the farmers. I was amused at an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on January 27 of this year, when the Tribune suggests that the farmers will have many questions to ask of these educators who are going around the country. I will refer to only the last one. It was that the farmers will probably ask the tax officials for assurance that the money they are paying in income tax is being used providently and economically. I think the farmers will want to know just that.
There is one other point I wish to make, if I may change over to it now, and that is with regard to the question of unemployment insurance. There are two points I want to raise in connection with this matter. This is definitely important to our town and city people in the west, and likely it is important all over Canada. First of all, a man or girl who is working is made to pay a certain amount week after week or month after month, as the case may be. Then there comes a time when this girl or man has reached a sufficient length of employment in point of time to entitle such person, if laid off or out of work, to the maximum benefits. I maintain that, after any employee reaches that point, he should no longer have to pay anything in to that fund and should be given, in effect, a

The Address-Mr. Miller
paid-up poli-cy in the fund until he or she has drawn something out of it. I do not think that would put the fund in an actuarially unsound position, because at the moment I think there is something like a $400 million surplus.
The other point 1 wish 'to make about unemployment insurance is this. I was astonished just a few weeks ago to have come into my office a man who had been ill, wras still ill, and was unable to work. He had worked for a long time and, had he not been sick', he would have been entitled to draw unemployment insurance benefits. However, he left his job, not to quit work but to go to a hospital and lie on his back for six or seven months. When he went in to collect unemployment insurance he was calmly and properly told by the officials that he was not entitled to draw any unemployment insurance because he had been sick in the hospital and unavailable for employment. That seems to be an utter disregard of the promises which were made to the people when this scheme was initiated. I think an amendment to the regulations or to the act should be put through whereby a man, if he is genuinely sick and unable to work by reason of sickness, should be entitled to draw his unemployment insurance for the same period as if he were available for work and there was none. Otherwise, to me it seems to be a mockery.
Another point that is of local interest to me is the question of rents on wartime housing. We have a number of those schemes in various places in my constituency, particularly in the city of Portage la Prairie. There should be a differentiation in the minds of the government between places like Portage la Prairie and some bigger centres like Toronto or Windsor. I say that for this reason. In the city of Portage la Prairie-and I use it as an example-most of the people, as I said before, are in the small income bracket. To me it seems incongruous and unfair that, in the city of Portage la Prairie, these young returned boys and 'their wives living in these houses and I am not criticizing the houses; they served a purpose and are serving a good purpose-who are earning likely from $85 to $150 a month, should be paying rent running from S22 to $30 a month, depending on the size of the house. In a community where the earning power is small or the salaries paid are small, I maintain it is not fair that such a large proportion of the small salary should go to provide shelter. It is not a proper percentage of salary. It might be proper in some other centre, but not in a city like Portage la Prairie. I urge the authorities to give this
matter consideration and maybe reduce the rate of rent in our community and others in a similar position.
I want to say a little about the agricultural situation. It seems to me 'that now, at long last, the farmers are realizing that the prices they are securing for their products are not fair ones having regard to the cost of the things which they have to buy. It is becoming increasingly evident, I think, throughout the country that they are desperately dissatisfied at the present time. I am not going to enter into a discussion of the wheat agreement or anything like that; I am just making the statement that they are becoming dissatisfied. That should be a warning to the government, and 'they should try to rectify that position.
The coarse grains situation is terrible. It has been discussed here time and time again, so that it is not necessary for me to go all over it, but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) gave an explanation which to me was far from, satisfactory. If I remember correctly he told us that everybody, every farmer, knew the ceiling price on coarse grains was going off in September, anyway, and that this action was delayed until October 22 only because of the packers' strike. In all fairness I must say the minister may be right when he says everyone knew, but I have made extensive inquiries, particularly among the farmers, and I have yet to find a single farmer who had any conception whatever that there was to be any change in the prices of coarse grains until the following August. When the minister says they knew I presume he must believe that is a correct statement, but I repeat that I cannot find any farmers who knew the ceiling was coming off in September, and that this was delayed simply because of the packers' strike.
There is also a rumour going around-I almost hesitate to mention this, and I emphasize that it is only a rumour-that in speaking to members of the federation in Ottawa some weeks ago the minister, in explaining the peculiar manner in which the ceiling wras taken off coarse grains, said he knew a delegation was coming from the old country to talk about food prices and food contracts, and that the coarse grains were thrown into the open market for the purpose of demonstrating to the Britishers who came over here that they were getting cheap food, and to show what would happen if the farmers were really given the world price in the open market. I hardly believe the Minister of Agriculture would put on a side show like that for the benefit of visitors from the old country, and
The Address-Mr. Miller

in doing so sacrifice the welfare, not only of the livestock industry, but also of the entire industry of agriculture throughout this country, both east and west. But I suggest that it is being rumoured in the locality where I move around that this was the explanation given; and I am told that one of those men who said he heard it accepted that as a perfectly logical and common-sense explanation. If that is a common-sense explanation I suggest that the federation should replace that particular officer, in any event.
I think most farmers agree that the Minister of Agriculture or somebody has bungled the whole situation as far as coarse grains are concerned from the point of view of the farmers, the livestock producers and everybody else. It has been bungled from beginning to end. With all the respect I have for the ability of the minister, I am afraid that if he remains in office for even the brief space of time during which I believe he will continue to occupy his present position he may, though unwillingly and unwittingly, preside over the liquidation of the industry of agriculture in this country'.
The western grumblers!

The western grumblers? I
think I am giving the views of the western grumblers better than the Minister of Agriculture has given them.
I doubt it.

There is one other point
with which I wish to deal rather quickly, if I may. I think at this time I am justified in commenting upon a condition which exists among ourselves, the people of this country, with respect "to some of the things thar have been done to take away from us our natural freedom. I am amazed at the attitude now taken by our own people with regard to the assumption by the government of almost dictatorial powers over their rights and freedoms. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, while we boast of our democratic way of life I believe we are in danger of losing our dearly earned and highly treasured freedom. That freedom is the hallmark of democracy as we know it. No enemy is taking our freedom from us; nevertheless we are losing it just as surely through our own lassitude. More and more our property and our liberty are falling under the absolute control of either government employees or ministers of the crown. These government employees have no responsibility whatever to the people; and I do not think even a minister of the crown has the right to take unto himself such wide and extensive powers.

What has happened to the courts? Now they are usually taken out of the picture. Usually someone not qualified so to do sits in judgment upon us, either without a right of appeal or with a right of appeal so expensive that none of us can take advantage of it. I maintain that our courts were established by the people for their own protection, but the functions of our courts are being usurped more and more by officials. Many people think statements like this are just the rantings of another lawyer. That, as I said a moment ago, is the attitude which amazes me; that we do not worry more about the fact that we are losing those freedoms. We Canadians sit back complacently and say, "This is a free country. We have always been free and we always will be free." We forget that we have this freedom simply and solely because it was won for us through the struggles of our forebears. It is not something we have acquired by ourselves and for ourselves. It was acquired by others who suffered that we might have it. But, as has been said here previously by others more competent than I, we have grown so accustomed to freedom that we cannot even contemplate the possibility of losing it. Let us remember that within our memory and within our time other countries thought exactly the same thing, and that within the last ten or fifteen years peoples of other countries have seen their freedom vanish, to be regained only by further struggles and sacrifices. Many of our liberties in this country already have been curtailed, and this has occurred so gradually that none of us has noticed it creeping upon us, and none has really noticed his loss. More and more our statutes, both federal and provincial, provide that instead of a man being held innocent until proved guilty, which is the basic theory of British justice, he is now forced to prove himself innocent in our courts of law. Many statutes also provide that a man who innocently does a prohibited act is guilty of an offence by reason of the mere contravention of a statute, notwithstanding the fact that one of our great basic rules of freedom and liberty is that no man shall be convicted of an offence unless he commits a wrongful act with wrongful intent. Now a man can be found guilty of an offence because of the contravention of a regulation, and fined or sent to jail. Some of these regulations are not even made by parliament; they are made by committees and boards.
All these things are bad enough, but in addition I am afraid-and I do not like this-

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
that some people are beginning to suspect, though they may do so unfairly and unjustly, that political friends get favoured treatment while he who is without friends at court can whistle and like it.
Oh, oh.

I am not accusing anybody or any group; I say I believe that feeling is spreading in our country, and it is not good. There is no use trying to laugh it off. It is there. Let us go out and try to correct it. Canadians should fight these many encroachments on their liberty. The trouble is that nobody bothers or gets excited until he has had his own toes trampled upon. Some day it will be too late. We may laugh and be incredulous now, but some day we shall awaken to the astounding reality that much of that traditional liberty which was so dearly bought has slipped away from us beyond recall.
The latest example of encroachment upon our liberties is the giving to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) of this government widespread powers. He becomes the czar of all the czars, and even though the present minister may be the fairest man in public office, yet the office which he represents is being invested with powers which are too wide, powers so wide that we who hope to continue to live in a democracy should, at least in my humble judgment, rise up and protest. He has the power of life and death over industry, and even though the present minister who has received this power, or is going to receive it, might not do so, someone in the future, whom we cannot now know, may use this tremendous power to crush the business life out of his political enemies. That is a sorry position, and I maintain we should not even be placed in a position where that might be possible. It is too serious. However, the citizens as a whole do not become alarmed any more because, obviously, we cannot conceive that we shall ever lose our liberty. Nevertheless, these steadily increasing encroachments will in due course encompass our ruin.
Responsible government officials, crown officers and so on, defend all these statutes and encroachments by saying that the integrity of our crown prosecutors and the high sense of public duty of officials who administer the law constitute our assurance that there will be no miscarriage of justice, no loss of freedom and no abuses of the wide powers given to these people. The answer to that, even if such a defence were acceptable, is that it is still impractically dangerous to part from the
safeguards which, from wide experience, have been placed around our liberties, and to replace those safeguards with the pious hope that government employees or party officials or ministers of any political stripe, invested with excessive powers, will act wisely or fairly.
Certainly I believe that no one in Canada should willingly relinquish the protection of our liberties embodied in the great principles of British justice and British parliamentary practice enshrined in the hearts of Britons everywhere, and which are regarded by all Canadians whom I know as the great heritage of one who calls himself a Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my genial friend the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller), particularly because in the first few minutes of his speech he referred to the high cost of living and the difficulty the people in his constituency were experiencing in that regard.
I was glad he made reference to that, because perhaps he has now struck on a policy which is not very different from that of the party to which I belong. I hold in my hand a quotation taken from the Winnipeg Tribune of October 19, 1946, which purports to have been taken from the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) at a time when he was taking part in the by-election in Portage la Prairie at which the hon. member was elected. I hope these words are not prophetic, because this is what the leader of the opposition said in relation to the issue of the cost of living:
Mr. Miller's election will have no effect whatever on government controls because Inis views, stated on every platform, are in entire accord with the government's stated plan.
I am sorry the hon. member was given such a poor start because, in effect, the leader of the opposition said that, whether the present hon. member was elected or not, it would make no difference whatsoever so far as government policy is concerned, because he is in full accord with it. The hon. member may say, "After all, that was not my own statement"; but it was the statement of the leader of the opposition.
However, I have also his own statement made just one day earlier, on October 18, in which he is reported in the Portage la Prairie Graphic as having said this:
Mr. Miller emphasized there was no difference between the Liberals and Progressive Conservatives on price control and inflation.
I will leave it at that, because I hope to come back to the policy of that party later in my speech. I do not say that in any spirit of
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny

oarping criticism, but merely to point out that it is sometimes convenient not to make statements of that kind during a by-election when there is a chance of one's speaking later on the floor of the House of Commons.
Regardless of the many important issues which could be discussed at this time, there can be no doubt at all in the mind of anyone, irrespective of where he sits, that the issue uppermost in the minds of people throughout the country and members of the House of Commons is that of price control and the cost of living. I do not think there is any use in fooling ourselves that we can side-track public opinion any longer by talking about incidental matters in the house. I believe the great majority, perhaps seventy-five per cent or more, of the people in the country who sent us here, expect that during this session of parliament in 1948, before we go home, we shall do something about the cost of living. And I serve notice that the people will not be satisfied with the setting up of a committee to study the question, if that is all that is to be done.
In a recent poll of public opinion about a month ago it was reported that seventy-six per cent of the people of Canada were in favour of the re-establishment of price controls. That makes it the issue of the day. I do not think there was ever a time, certainly not since the election of 1945, when seventy-five per cent of the people of Canada expressed themselves as being agreed upon the necessity of taking a certain step at any time. I believe that this is the last gasp for those members of the Liberal party who are private members and who, like myself, are sometimes referred to as the backbenchers. They have sat session after session without offering criticism; and I am sure I speak accurately when I say that at times they have ground their teeth at some of the government's policies brought down. But through it all they have faithfully and dutifully stood by and voted for the government in order to maintain it in office.
On this one occasion I believe the government should declare an open vote on the amendment before the house so as to permit private members of the Liberal party to express their opinions on this very important question of price controls; because if they do not declare themselves now I believe they will find a very warm reception awaiting them upon their return to their constituencies; perhaps a little warmer than they expect. I do not say that in order to frighten them; but every member of the house to whom I have spoken tells me his files are bulging with letters and resolutions from various bodies

throughout the country demanding, requesting and urging that something be done immediately about this question of prices.
I shall not quote the resolutions and letters I have received; it would take too long. But I shall refer to the bodies which sent them. For example, these include the various branches of the Canadian Legion; the united electrical radio and machine workers of America; the Winnipeg labour council; the Canadian Congress of Labour, the brotherhood of express employees; the trades and labour council of Winnipeg; the dominion civil servants of Vancouver; the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks; the express and freight handlers; the Winnipeg general hospital employees ; the Canadian association of consumers -and a whole string of farm organizations and co-operatives too long to mention. That is the almost unanimous expression of opinion from the people we are here to represent. This is no disgruntled minority looking for a concession. It is the people of Canada who are speaking to their representatives in plain language and asking them to do something in this house; and I believe that before we disperse for the session we should be able to show something in the way of legislation and say: We have answered the call of the people of Canada.
What is the government doing about the matter? I think the hon. member for Portage la Prairie was correct when he said that, no matter what views and policies the various parties may hold on this question, the government for the moment are responsible for taking action within the life of this parliament, and it is up to the government to take the initiative. What are they going to do? We were given an indication of what they may do by the Prime Minister's announcement that a resolution will be introduced to set up a committee of the house to study the price question. This is not the time for setting up committees to study a question which requires immediate action.
There may be some members of the house who sat on the price spreads committee of fourteen years ago, which reported in 1934. I have some figures here gathered by that committee which I shall give later. The work of the committee was later transferred to a royal commission. The figures gathered prove that at that time profiteering was going on undoubtedly on a large scale. That was fourteen years ago. So the government cannot say that they have not been warned or that they have not the material facts upon which to base action. I have three large volumes here embodying the work of that commission.

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
They were kindly given to me by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), perhaps because he had no room for them in his own office, or because he may have thoroughly digested them. These volumes give the data gathered and they contain a mine of information. So the government have all the evidence they require, if they are looking for profiteers, to get down to business.
I notice that the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) is reported in the Toronto Star as having said that the government will turn the searchlight on those people who are profiteering. These were his words:
The government intends to turn the searchlight on those people who have profiteered as a result of the goverment taking off price controls, and they are going to have to face the eventualities of price profiteering at the expense of the people.
That is an excellent statement but it comes about fourteen years late. Further on, he said:
We as Liberals admit we made a mistake, so we have put the controls back on again.
Where?

The question is obvious: what controls? The government are just kidding themselves if they believe they have re-introduced price control.
I think the one class of people who have the most to complain about are the farmers. In western Canada the farmers for many years were promised stabilization. The organized farmers, the pools and co-operatives of various kinds agreed with the government that stabilization was the objective to be striven for, and we did achieve a certain amount of stabilization during the war. The bulk contracts with Great Britain for meat, grain, eggs and other products did bring an assured price to the farmer which acted as a floor price, but at the present time that floor price is acting as the ceiling price. The farmer is selling his wheat, his eggs and his meat products at ceiling prices to Great Britain. While those prices are not bad as compared with what prices used to be, the farmer has a legitimate complaint because the prices of all the products he has to use in his operations are going up day by day, and no one knows how high they will go. Take the price of gasoline, oil, farm implements of all kinds and the tools the farmer uses in his operations; the prices of all these things are going up day by day, and as a consequence the farmer is in a very uncertain position.
We had a long discussion before the Christmas recess of the feed grain situation and how that was handled. That one blunder by the government threw the whole livestock
production industry into complete chaos, and it had no sooner begun to revive than it was faced with sharp increases in the prices of all the articles the farmer has to buy, while the prices of the goods he sells are fixed by the agreements and by the fact that he cannot ship his produce across the line into the United States. It almost seems to me that somebody in the government is deliberately trying to upset the stabilization program which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) from time to time advocates in this house. It w'ould appear that someone was trying to sabotage the efforts at stabilization which the minister has told us so often he is making. As a matter of fact, I have often heard criticism of the Minister of Agriculture which was not justified. Heaven knows there is enough legitimate criticism coming to him, but there were times when criticism that should have been directed at the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) -was actually loaded on to the Minister of Agriculture. It put me in mind of the story of the lady who brought her little boy to school for the first time. She told the teacher he was a very sensitive child and gave her a long list of instructions how to handle little Douglas. She said, "If Douglas does anything wrong you must not punish him; just slap Jimmie next to him, and you will frighten him in that way." That seems to have been what was happening sometimes when criticism was directed against the Minister of Agriculture.
The farmers of western Canada have been very patient. I believe they have made an intelligent approach to this question of prices. They are one occupational group-there may be others-which did not seek to take advantage of the world shortage of food. If ever there wras a time when there was a chance for profiteering in this world it was in this time of shortages. But the farmers of western Canada are close to the soil; they know something about the production of food and of how much work it requires to make a living, and they have a great deal of sympathy for the population of the world and were satisfied to take what they thought was a fair price, even though they were tempted and are still tempted by the Winnipeg grain exchange and other bodies which dangle $3 wheat and things of that sort in front of them. But the farmers are practical people and they say this: Not only shall we serve the needs of humanity better if we take a reasonable price for our food products now and have a stabilized market now and for the future, but it will be in our own best interests in the long run if we do not gouge our customers. So they
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny

were prepared to accept prices that were reasonable, provided that they were in proper relationship to other prices. But now they see all other prices going sky-high, and even the most patient farmer finds his patience becoming exhausted. They are justified in saying to the government: You offer us stabilization with the one hand, and then you give us confusion and chaos with the other. I believe if nothing is done about prices in the next few months there is a real danger, not only of a great loss in potential production on the farm, but of non-delivery strikes such as have taken place in the past, resulting in general dislocation.
There are those who say: Prices are high because wages are high. I have plenty of evidence here, if the house will hear it, to show that wages are not the cause of high prices today. For example, one report taken from the figures of the bureau of statistics shows that in 1946 Canadian corporations made a profit of $61 out of every man, woman and child in this country as compared with only $31 in 1938. It goes on to show that the total profit figure of these corporations was $3,059 million, and during the same period of time figures are quoted here to show that the real wages, that is the real purchasing power of the workers, farmers and salaried people in Canada dropped by eight per cent. In other words, it is quite clear that it is profiteering which is creating the high prices. That is even more serious than if it were wages or salaries which were doing it, because there would be a tendency for wages and salaries to find a certain level, even if it were high, and then stop there; but there is no level at which profiteering will stop. If they can make 100 per cent profit today, tomorrow they want 125 per cent. If they can get away with that, the next day they want 150 per cent.
I hold in my hand a pamphlet which, going back to 1938, shows the cost of producing a tractor. These figures are taken from a survey of the federal trade commission of the United States. It shows that out- of every $100 spent in producing a tractor, only $51'3, or 51*3 per cent, represents the cost of material, which includes also factory overhead and freight. The remainder amounts to 48-7 per cent of the selling cost, which includes the manufacturer's profit, the dealer's margin, advertising and so on. If it costs almost as much, within a few cents on a dollar to sell a tractor as it does to build it and ship it, then there is something seriously wrong with an economic system which operates in that way. As a matter of fact, out of $100 in the production 
of this tractor, direct labour received only $4-80. Therefore no one can say it is wages that are pushing up prices.
The hon. member who preceded me referred to the condition in which people who are on fixed income find themselves. I hold in my hand The Legionary, which is a publication of the Canadian Legion. In this publication they point out that the proposed increases to those on pension and those who are receiving allowances are far too small. I shall quote just a paragraph or two to show their point of view. On page 10 we find the following.
What is the date of the issue?

February, 1948. It
arrived today. I quote:
The general opinion regarding the government's proposals is that the}' are not sufficiently adequate to offset the rising cost of living. Furthermore, no provision has been made to increase the additional pension provided for wives and children or the pensions of other dependents entitled under the act.
It goes on to say further:	.
... to many pensioners and to all war veterans allowance recipients the tremendous increase in actual living costs is nothing less than catastrophic.
That is only one example. One could go on and quote letters and resolutions from old age pensioners, from other people on fixed incomes and from people who are not even provided for because, let us not forget, that while we are worrying about the purchasing power of those who are on pension, there are thousands of people in this country who should be on pension but are not. There are crippled adults in every province. For example, in Manitoba there is no provincial legislation to provide any financial assistance to crippled adults. They become a charge on the municipality in which they live, and quite often they live in a municipality which has difficulty in keeping up its roads, its schools and its bridges, and has nothing with which to finance people in that category. There are people who are between sixty-five and seventy years of age who, because of poor health, some through rheumatism or arthritis, some through paralysis or something of that sort, are completely disabled and who cannot apply for old age pension, but find themselves in a desperate position. The recent increase in the cost of living hits them all the harder because they have so much less to live on.
I want to refer to the position taken by the official opposition in this house on the question of price controls, as I said I would do. I am

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
speaking of our friends the Progressive Conservatives. Let me say at the outset that I am not saying this because I want to engage in a quarrel with them, but because of the motion which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) attempted to have adopted in the house the other day asking for the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the high cost of living. I was glad he moved the motion; I was sorry it was not acceptable; but I was surprised at the same time, because if any party in this house has a record for advocating decontrol it is certainly the Progressive Conservative party.
Not the way the government did it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No; you wanted it faster.

The hon. member for Trinity says, "Not the way the government did it"; but the only difference in the way the government did it and the way the Progressive Conservatives would have done it is that the government did it more slowly. To prove the accuracy of that statement, I am going to turn to the record. We can always depend on the record whenever there is a dispute. On March 5, 1947, this matter was discussed in this house, and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart), who was in the house a few moments ago, had this to say. which will be found at page 1059 of Hansard. Referring to the wartime prices and trade board, he said:
We have an army of men of various types running around the country doing a useless job, and it is about time they were put on the production end. I have reference to employees of the wartime prices and trade board.
Further on, he warmed up to his speech and said:
If the small businessmen of this country have to put up with this kind of thing, it is time that somebody took a sawed-off shotgun and started to work.
That is decontrol with a vengeance. Further on, he had this to say:
For goodness sake, let us get back to normal. Let the law of supply and demand hold sway.
Well, we got it faster than he expected. The law of supply and demand did hold sway for a time, and then what happened? Then his own leader rises in his place in the house and moves an adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance because the law of supply and demand has held sway.
I have no objection to anyone being for decontrol. They have a perfect right to do
so; but if a party in this house in one session of parliament advocates decontrol, and then in the next session of parliament complains because they got it, there is something wrong somewhere. I am not going to suggest that we run for the sawed-off shotgun or anything of that sort, but I will say this. It is easy enough for members of the Progressive Conservative opposition to get up in this house and blindly state that if government controls were removed the law of supply and demand would soon bring us back to normal. Surely they realize by now that for every law, so-called, of supply and demand, there are a dozen economic lawyers whose chief purpose seems to be to stymie its efforts, to destroy free competition, to restrict production, to obstruct trade, all of which are the essential elements in the creation of monopoly.
The Progressive Conservatives were not the only party that advocated decontrol. Our friends the Social Crediters are on record by a statement of their own leader on March 21:
Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned control.
That is, state socialism.
If they prefer unplanned control that is their business.
How about the Bretton Woods agreement, which you supported?
I am not the author, either of the Bretton Woods agreement or of Social Credit unplanned control. I am merely stating what is on record and if it is not palatable to my hon. friend-
Be consistent with yourself.

-then it is his trouble and not mine. But so much for the parties in the house. I do not need to refer to the policy of the government itself or of the party that supports the government because their action speaks for itself. They have talked controls but have decontrolled full steam ahead while doing so. But what about other organizations outside parliament who give us advice once in a while? I have a statement of March 26, 1947, by the president of the Robert Simpson Company, which is the same as we hear from the official opposition. That gentleman said:
An over-all and immediate lifting of ceilings would quickly react to the benefit of all consumers.
An hon. member beside me says. "Particularly Simpson's", and he is right to the hilt, because I have an excerpt from the price spreads report of 1934 which shows something of the history of the Robert Simpson Company. The president says that all consumers would
